To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
Ireland is a country where a significant number of women are not entitled to social security payments, even though they are in employment and are the partners of social security recipients.
Ireland has a significant number of working aged partners of social welfare recipients who are excluded from the labour market and who face a variety of barriers to employment.
Ireland has a significant group of invisible women who are partners of coupled social security recipients.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the invisibility of qualified adults, a group of women whose numbers have risen sharply during the economic downturn.
a group of women who are largely ignored in policy and academic debates.
a group of women who are largely hidden in Irish society and who are the subject of a significant policy failure.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the policy architecture in Ireland is not fit for purpose, and that it is not in the best interests of Irish society, Irish women or the Irish economy to continue to ignore this group of women.
the Irish government has failed to address the issue of qualified adults and that this is not a sustainable situation.
the Irish State has failed to adequately respond to the crisis of the Great Recession in relation to partners, and that it is now time to address this failure and to reform the system.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the current system is not only unjust but also inefficient, and that it is time to move on from a policy approach that is based on a model of the family that no longer exists.
the current policy architecture offers clear patriarchal dividends for male partners and employers and the policy makers.
Ireland’s policy response to the crisis is a missed opportunity to address a long-standing and significant problem in Irish social security.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the invisibility of qualified adult social security claimants is not an accident.

Ireland has a unique opportunity to reform its welfare system in a way that would benefit both women and children and to move beyond the outdated concept of wifely labor and the gendered division of labour.
Ireland’s partners have been left behind in policy terms, but they have been very visible in our research and in their own lives.
